title: How to read this book?
text:
Practical checklists and maintenance notes for setting up a home, gardening on a balcony or small plot, and keeping a road bike in good working order.
The book is organised in three parts:

Gardening and planting — containers, substrate, crops, herb care on an east-facing balcony, and basic tools.
Interior DIY and equipment — room-by-room shopping and setup lists for moving in.
Bicycle maintenance — anatomy, brakes, gears, wheels and tyres, and steering adjustment.

All lists use GitHub-style task checkboxes (- [ ] / - [x]) so you can tick items off as you go.

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
3.1 Site and watering
Notes for culinary herbs on a ground-floor, east-facing balcony in Marseille (Provençal south): strong morning sun, shade from midday onwards, hot dry summers, mild winters, and occasional Mistral.
The morning sun is enough for Mediterranean herbs without the scorching west-facing afternoon that burns basil and parsley in July and August. Keep thyme in a separate, drier pot; grow basil, curly parsley, chives, and dill in richer, moister compost.
crumbs: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
Orientation: east — water in the evening in midsummer, or in the morning after the first hour of sun. Avoid wetting leaves in full sun.
Wind: ground floor is calmer than upper storeys, but still shelter dill and basil from a strong Mistral with the wall or a light screen.
Drainage: every pot needs holes and a saucer; empty standing water after watering so roots do not sit in a puddle.
Summer rhythm: basil and parsley almost daily in a heatwave; chives every two days; thyme twice a week at most.
crumbs: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
3.2 Basil
(basilic)

Light / heat: morning sun; afternoon shade in Marseille is an advantage. Bring the pot in if nights drop below about 10 °C.
Water: keep the compost evenly moist, never waterlogged. Wilt in the afternoon is a cue to water that evening.
Humidity: mist leaves in very dry Mistral weather; good air around the plant still matters (do not crowd).
Support: none. See Trimming below.
Companions: curly parsley and chives in the same wide pot. Keep thyme out of this mix.


3.2.1 Trimming basil for harvest
Follow the node-and-pair method from Les Sourciers — how to prune basil. Leaves sit in pairs on the stem; at each node, small axillary buds can become new stems if you give them light.

Wait until the main stem has at least two well-formed leaf pairs with visible side buds.
Cut just above a pair of buds, leaving almost no stub (a long stub tends to rot).
Prefer the second pair from the base for the first cut, so the lower buds can thicken.
Each cut yields two new stems; repeat the same cut on those stems as they lengthen. That is how a single spike becomes a bush.
Use the leafy tip you removed. Do not strip single leaves from the lower stem — that is what produces a “bald stick”.

Flowering does not reverse if you keep cutting: the plant has already switched. Stagger a second sowing for a continuous leaf crop. Flowering tops are still edible (oil, drying); the leaves remain edible but thinner.






flowchart TD
  A[Main stem with 2+ leaf pairs] --> B[Cut just above a node]
  B --> C[Two axillary shoots grow]
  C --> D[Repeat on each new stem]
  D --> E[Bushy plant + harvested tips]




Figure 3.2: Basil: cut above a leaf-pair node so two side shoots take over.
crumbs: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
3.3 Chives
(ciboulette)

Light: morning sun; tolerates the east-facing shade later in the day.
Water: moderate — let the top centimetre dry, then water.
Care: see Trimming below. Divide clumps in spring if the pot is packed.
Support: none. A clump in a 15–20 cm pot is enough.
Companions: basil and parsley (they like similar moisture).


3.3.1 Trimming chives for harvest
Treat it like a haircut, as in Les Sourciers — how to prune chives: cut the whole tuft, do not pluck a few tubes.

First cut when the leaves are about 15 cm.
In spring and summer, cut every two weeks.
Shear a few centimetres above the soil with scissors or secateurs. Leave that stub so the plant can regrow; cutting flush often yellows the new shoots.
In autumn, one shorter cut helps it into winter. In a Marseille winter you can keep harvesting lightly; if a hard frost is forecast, stop cutting and mulch the crown.
If the clump is dense and stays wet, divide it: lift a wedge with roots and pot it on. Crowded, uncut chives hold moisture and can rot.

Use the cut leaves fresh, freeze in portions, or dry. The purple flowers are edible.






flowchart TD
  A[Leaves ~15 cm] --> B[Shear 2–3 cm above soil]
  B --> C[Regrowth in ~2 weeks]
  C --> B
  B --> D[Divide if the clump is packed]




Figure 3.3: Chives: shear the tuft a few centimetres above the crown.
crumbs: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
3.4 Thyme
(thym)

Light: the most sun-hungry of this list; place at the brightest edge of the balcony.
Water: spare. Allow the compost to dry between waterings. Overwatering in a saucer is the usual way to lose thyme here.
Substrate: grittier mix (potting compost plus sand or fine gravel). No rich nitrogen feed.
Support: none. See Trimming below.
Companions: grow alone. It wants drier roots than basil, parsley, and dill.


3.4.1 Trimming thyme for harvest
Thyme lignifies: old brown wood will not resprout.

Snip green tips only, just above a leaf node, as if taking cuttings. Never cut back into bare wood.
After flowering, a light all-over trim of the green growth keeps the mound dense.
Do not “mow” the plant to a stump. If it becomes woody and sparse, start a new plant from a tip cutting rather than hard-pruning.
Harvest little and often through the growing season; a large one-off cut in midsummer can kill a pot-grown plant in heat.
crumbs: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
3.5 Dill
(aneth)

Light: morning sun; it bolts (runs to flower) fast in Marseille heat, so successive small sowings work better than one large plant.
Water: regular, like parsley; do not let the pot bake.
Support: stems are brittle — a thin cane or a ring of string once the plant is above about 30 cm.
Care: see Trimming below.
Companions: own pot. Dill can inhibit some neighbours and grows tall enough to shade basil.


3.5.1 Trimming dill for harvest
Dill is a short-lived annual. You harvest foliage; you cannot turn it into a perennial bush like basil.

Take young leaves by snipping whole side stems, not by stripping the main axis bald.
For a leaf crop, cut before the flower umbel opens — flavour drops and the plant then puts energy into seed.
Leave one plant to flower if you want seeds (pickles) or to feed hoverflies.
In Marseille heat it bolts fast: sow a pinch every two to three weeks rather than relying on one plant.
When a stem is for the vase or the kitchen, cut it near the base; the remaining seedlings in the pot will take over.
crumbs: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony

title: 3  Herb care on an east-facing balcony
text:
3.6 Curly parsley
(persil frisé)

Light: morning sun and afternoon shade suit it; it scorches in full south or west sun in July.
Water: never let the compost dry out. Deep pot (taproot): 20 cm or more.
Humidity: appreciates a light mist in dry wind, like basil.
Support: none. See Trimming below.
Companions: basil and chives. Slow to germinate — buy a seedling if you want a crop this month.


3.6.1 Trimming curly parsley for harvest
Parsley grows from a central crown. If you cut that, the plant stops.

Always take outer stems, cutting them at the base (soil level), not halfway up the stalk.
Leave the inner, paler shoots — they are next week’s leaves.
Harvest regularly; neglected plants send up a flower stalk (biennial) and then the leaf quality falls.
If a flower stalk appears, cut it out at the base unless you want seed. Start a replacement pot: parsley in a container is not worth keeping once it has bolted in summer heat.

title: 5  Bike overview and equipment
text:
5.1 Essential toolkit
General anatomy notes and the toolkit required for routine maintenance.
Figure 5.1 is the published contents of the Decathlon 900 box: FR: dérive-chaîne. Punch that drives a chain pin in or out so the chain can be shortened or opened. The Decathlon 900 box covers 6–11 speeds.chain tool (6–11 speed), hex keys, Torx T10–T30, FR: fouet à chaîne. Tool with a length of chain that holds the cassette still while the lockring is undone.chain whip, Shimano HG FR: démonte-cassette (Shimano HG). Splined tool that fits the cassette lockring; turned anti-clockwise to remove. Distinct from a freewheel remover (démonte-roue-libre).lockring tool, and a FR: plateau. Toothed ring bolted to the crank; the front half of the gearing (e.g. 52/39/30 on a triple).chainring nut wrench. Check the physical box before buying extras — the listed hex set often stops at 8 mm.
Buy in addition: a 10 mm hex and a FR: clé dynamométrique. Wrench that clicks or indicates at a set newton-metre value. Needed for an FSA self-extracting crank bolt (about 38–41 Nm).torque wrench that reaches at least 41 Nm. Quick-link pliers and grease are comfort, not strict necessities.

5.1.1 Torque wrench note
For an FSA 30 mm axle with a self-extracting bolt, FSA specifies a 10 mm hex and 38–41 Nm with a calibrated wrench.
A compact 4–24 Nm wrench with a 10 mm bit is excellent for derailleurs and chainring bolts but does not reach crank-bolt torque. Prefer a 3/8″ or 1/4″+3/8″ wrench covering roughly 5–50 Nm or 5–60 Nm with a 10 mm hex bit.

title: 6  Brakes

6.2 How to monitor rim brakes

Pad thickness — replace before the metal holder contacts the rim.
Pad alignment — toe-in slightly at the leading edge; full contact without rubbing the tyre.
Rim wear — look for a wear groove disappearing or a concave profile.
Cable and housing — smooth lever travel; no fraying at the end.
Quick test — wheel spins freely off the stand; firm lever feel with ~2–3 cm travel before firm contact.

title: 7  Gears
text:
Height and alignment — outer cage plate ~2 mm above the big chainring teeth; cage parallel to the chainrings.
Limit screws — with the cable slack:

L (low / inner) — loosen to move toward the frame (e.g. if it sits on the middle ring instead of the inner); tighten to move outward if the chain drops off the inner ring.
H (high / outer) — sets the outer limit on the big ring.

Cable tension — leave ~2 turns of barrel-adjuster range; if shifts to larger rings are sluggish, increase cable tension; if the chain overshoots, reduce tension.

title: 7  Gears
text:
7.2 Rear derailleur
Reference: VCMB rear derailleur guide.






Figure 7.2: Rear derailleur adjustment walkthrough.




Confirm the derailleur hanger is straight and the cage aligns with the sprockets.
H limit (high gear, smallest sprocket) — turning out (anti-clockwise) moves the upper jockey wheel outward; turning in moves it toward the frame.
L limit (low gear, largest sprocket) — the opposite sense to H: turning in moves outward; turning out moves toward the frame. (The L screw is sometimes called the “high stop” in shop jargon — confusing, but common.)
Cable tension — middle chainring, smallest sprocket; increase tension if upshifts are hesitant, decrease if the chain climbs too eagerly.
B-tension screw — sets gap between upper jockey wheel and largest sprocket.

  A[Smallest sprocket — set H limit] --> B[Largest sprocket — set L limit]
  B --> C[Set B-tension screw]
  C --> D[Clamp cable on middle chainring / small sprocket]
  D --> E[Index through all 10 sprockets]
  E --> F{Skipping or noise?}
  F -->|Yes| G[Barrel adjuster ± quarter turn]
  F -->|No| H[Done]

text:
7.4 How to change the mechanical components

7.4.1 Pedal removal first
The left pedal sits on the opposite side of the bottom bracket shell (i.e. on your left when you mount the bike).






Figure 7.6: Which way to turn a screw




Fitting: the right pedal tightens clockwise; the left pedal tightens anti-clockwise.
Removal: the right pedal loosens anti-clockwise (the opposite of normal right-hand threads).







flowchart LR
  R[Right crank] -->|tighten| CW1[Clockwise]
  R -->|loosen| ACW1[Anti-clockwise]
  L[Left crank] -->|tighten| ACW2[Anti-clockwise]
  L -->|loosen| CW2[Clockwise]




Figure 7.7: Pedal thread directions (viewed from the outside of the crank).







7.4.2 Crankset removal second
Traditional square-taper or external-bearing systems use a crank extractor; FSA 30 mm self-extracting axles use a 10 mm hex in the central bolt instead — see Section 7.4.3 for sprocket clusters, and the self-extracting procedure below for the FSA crank.
For extractor-type cranks:

Remove the chain.
Remove the retaining bolt at the base of the crank.
Fit the crank extractor; if stiff, back the extractor off slightly and tap with a mallet.
Tighten the extractor with a 14 mm spanner until the crank releases. Repeat on both sides, turning anti-clockwise.

Table 7.1: Mechanical differences between a threaded freewheel and a cassette.



Visual check (wheel off, turn the sprockets by hand):

Freewheel: a ring between the axle and the smallest sprocket stays still while the sprockets spin. The cluster is one block.
Cassette: the whole stack turns together; nothing stays fixed next to the axle. Nine sprockets or more is always a cassette.

7.4.3.1 Removing a cassette
The sprockets slide off the freehub body after the lockring is undone. The Decathlon 900 box already has the whip and the HG lockring tool.






Figure 7.13: Cassette removal on a Shimano HG freehub.




Remove the rear wheel and the quick-release or thru-axle.
Wrap the FR: fouet à chaîne. Tool with a length of chain that holds the cassette still while the lockring is undone.chain whip on the largest sprocket to stop the cassette turning.
Seat the FR: démonte-cassette (Shimano HG). Splined tool that fits the cassette lockring; turned anti-clockwise to remove. Distinct from a freewheel remover (démonte-roue-libre).lockring tool in the lockring.
Turn the lockring anti-clockwise.
Slide the sprockets off the splines (note the wider spline gap — it keys the orientation).
Clean the freehub body before refitting; tighten the new lockring clockwise.

 






flowchart LR
  A[Remove rear wheel] --> B[Remove quick-release / thru-axle]
  B --> C[Wrap chain whip on largest sprocket]
  C --> D[Insert HG lockring tool]
  D --> E[Turn lockring anti-clockwise]
  E --> F[Slide cassette off splines]
  F --> G[Clean freehub body]




Figure 7.14: Cassette removal on a Shimano HG freehub.







7.4.3.2 Removing a freewheel
The whole body unscrews from the hub. A cassette lockring tool will not fit: you need a freewheel remover whose splines (or two prongs) match that brand.

Same as above: wheel off, chain whip on the largest sprocket.
Seat the freewheel remover fully in the centre.
Turn anti-clockwise. The first break of thread is often very tight (pedalling has been tightening it for years).
Once loose, unscrew the whole body by hand.

Refit by starting the thread by hand, clockwise, square to the hub, then finish with the remover or by pedalling. Cross-threading ruins the hub.






flowchart LR
  A[Remove rear wheel] --> B[Chain whip on large sprocket]
  B --> C[Seat freewheel remover]
  C --> D[Turn anti-clockwise]
  D --> E[Unscrew whole body]




Figure 7.15: Threaded freewheel removal.

title: 7  Gears
text:
7.5 Summary infographic






flowchart TD
  A[Chain on small ring + small sprocket] --> B[Remove chain]
  B --> C[Remove rear derailleur — note cable clamp only]
  C --> D[Mount new RD — leave cable detached]
  D --> E[Set H limit before cabling]
  E --> F[Remove crank with 10 mm hex — self-extracting FSA]
  F --> G[Photograph washer stack]
  G --> H[Swap 52/39/30 chainrings on bench]
  H --> I[Light grease on bolt threads]
  I --> J[Reinstall crank — torque 38–41 Nm]
  J --> K[Adjust rear derailleur cable + limits + B screw]
  K --> L[Fit new 10-speed chain to old length]
  L --> M[Static shifts then test ride]




Figure 7.16: Chainring and rear-derailleur replacement (keep shifters, cables, FD).





Step-by-step:

Remove the chain — quick-link pliers if fitted; otherwise use the chain tool from the 900 box.
Remove the rear derailleur — slacken the cable pinch bolt only; no need to pull the inner wire from the shifter. Unbolt from the hanger (8–10 Nm on refit).
Set the H limit on the new derailleur before attaching the cable.
Remove the FSA crank — left side: 10 mm hex in the central self-extracting bolt, turn anti-clockwise. Do not remove the outer retaining ring; it is part of the extraction mechanism.
Photograph washers — especially the wave washer; keep the BB30 bearings in the frame.
Replace chainrings on the bench — use the chainring nut tool; orient markings and anti-drop pin on the outer ring behind the crank arm.
Grease bolt threads lightly — follow torque specs supplied with the new rings.
Reinstall the crank — restore washers in the original order; torque the 30 mm axle bolt to 38–41 Nm with a calibrated wrench.
Adjust the rear derailleur — H limit, cable tension, L limit, B-tension.
Fit a new 10-speed chain — match the old link count if the previous length was correct; respect directional markings.
Test — the front derailleur should need little change if tooth counts stay 52/39/30.

title: 7  Gears
text:
7.6 Zoom on Ultegra gear shift
The right-hand FR: manette STI (Shimano Total Integration). Combined brake lever and gear shifter on drop bars.STI lever indexes the rear derailleur; the left indexes the front. These notes cover a 10-speed Shimano lever of the same generation as the 105 triple above. Bar-clamp and cable work overlap with Section 6.3.






Figure 7.17: Servicing a right-hand Shimano 105 ST-5600 FlightDeck STI lever



Figure 7.17 is a workshop teardown of a right-hand 105 ST-5600 FlightDeck lever. The ratchet and pawls are the same 10-speed STI architecture as Ultegra of that era. Open the lever only if indexing feels gritty after a cable change:

Keep the tiny spacers, star washer, and square lock washer together.
Clean grit with solvent; do not bend the fine pawl spring.
Relubricate the ratchet with a light oil film. Grease packs the pawls and makes shifts sticky.

Refit the hood and test every click plus brake return before wrapping the bar.






Figure 7.18: Exploded view and install sequence for a right-hand Ultegra dual-control lever



Figure 7.18 is the parts legend and install sequence. Mount the lever before cabling:

Peel the hood back to expose the clamp band.
Align both levers on the drops, then torque the clamp bolt to 6–8 Nm. Check that the body sits square on the bar before the final tighten.
Fit the brake inner first (1.6 mm inner, 5 mm outer), with the nipple fully seated in the lever.
Shift to the smallest sprocket, grease the pawl area with Shimano SIS SP41, then fit the gear inner (1.2 mm inner, 4 mm outer) into the cable hook unit.







Figure 7.19: Workshop sheet for mounting a right-hand Ultegra shifter and fitting cables



Figure 7.19 is a compact sheet of the same three blocks: clamp, brake cable, gear cable. Use it at the bench as a checklist; use Figure 7.18 when a part name or seating diagram is unclear.
Before wrapping the bar, confirm:

both levers travel fully, with clean upshifts and downshifts;
inners run freely and every outer-casing end is seated;
the hoods sit neatly and the levers are square to each other.

See Figure 7.17, Figure 7.18, Figure 7.19 for the teardown, the exploded install diagram, and the compact workshop sheet.

title: 8  Tyres and wheels
text:
8.1.1 Tools






Figure 8.1: Spoke wrench icon




FR: clé à rayon. Small spanner that fits spoke nipples; clockwise (from the rim) increases tension when truing a wheel.spoke wrench (correct size for your nipples)
Truing stand or frame as a guide
Dish gauge (optional) — checks rim centreing on the hub
Lateral indicator — measures lateral run-out (“dish” error in the sideways plane)







Figure 8.2: Truing stand and indicators





8.1.2 Truing procedure
Spoke nipples tighten clockwise (viewed from the rim), increasing tension.

Check for broken spokes; replace any that are damaged.
Bring overall tension up evenly before fine truing.
Correct run-out in groups of 3–4 spokes at a time:

If the rim pulls left, tighten right-side spokes and/or loosen left-side spokes.
Reverse for movement to the right.

Work in ¼ or ½ turn increments — never force a nipple to its limit.

Full tutorial: Le Cyclo — wheel truing

  B -->|Yes| C[Replace spoke & pre-tension]
  B -->|No| D[Equalise base tension]
  D --> E[Adjust 3–4 spokes near deviation]
  E --> F{Run-out acceptable?}
  F -->|No| E
  F -->|Yes| G[Check dish & spoke tension balance]

title: 8  Tyres and wheels
text:
8.2 Tyres

8.2.1 Size markings: ETRTO, French, and inch
Three conventions appear on sidewalls. They do not measure the same thing, which is why a “26 inch” tyre may not fit another “26 inch” rim. Prefer the FR: ETRTO / ISO 5775. International tyre and rim size: width in millimetres, then inner diameter in millimetres, e.g. 25-622. The reliable number when buying tyres or tubes.ETRTO pair (ISO 5775) when buying tyres or tubes: width (mm)–inner diameter (mm).






Figure 8.4: French, inch, and ETRTO tyre markings















System
Example
What the numbers mean
Typical use




French
700x25C
Nominal outer diameter ~700 mm × width ~25 mm; letter is the old width class
Road


Inch
26x2.1
Nominal outer diameter (inches) × width (inches)
Mountain, leisure


ETRTO / ISO
25-622
Inflated width (mm) – bead-seat / inner diameter (mm)
International, tubes





Table 8.1: How the three tyre-size conventions map onto one another.



The French system uses the tyre’s outer diameter; ETRTO uses the inner (bead-seat) diameter. That is why a road 700C and a mountain-bike 29er share 622 mm in ETRTO, and why 27.5" / 650B is 584 mm. Inch markings are the least precise: historically several incompatible “26 inch” bead seats existed.






Figure 8.5: ETRTO inner diameter versus French and inch names



Width on the sidewall is only a guide: the same tyre sits wider or narrower on a different internal rim width. Match the tyre to the internal rim width rather than the marketing size alone.






Figure 8.6: Tyre width versus internal rim width



For a 25 mm road tyre on a 622 mm bead, the sidewall should read something like 700×25C and 25-622. When in doubt, quote the ETRTO pair to the shop.


8.2.2 Routine checks

Correct inflation (see sidewall range; typically 6–8 bar / 80–115 psi for 25 mm road tyres)
Tread wear indicators or flat spot in the centre
Cuts, embedded glass, sidewall bulges
Valve seating (Presta: tighten lockring finger-tight only)

title: 9  Steering and headset
text:
9.1 Threaded headset adjustment
Headset adjustment (“steering play”) and related notes from personal maintenance logs.
Excess play is felt as a knock or looseness when rocking the bike with the front brake on.

title: 9  Steering and headset
text:
Figure 9.1: Threaded FR: jeu de direction. Bearing assembly that lets the fork steer in the head tube. Threaded (locknut plus adjusting cup) or threadless (star nut or compression plug plus stem).headset adjustment.




9.1.1 Adjustment sequence

Loosen the locknut (top nut).
Turn the adjusting cup / bearing race until play just disappears with the fork centred — the bars should turn smoothly without binding.
Hold the adjusting cup in place and re-tighten the locknut.
Re-check: no play, no notchiness.







flowchart TD
  A[Front brake on — rock bike] --> B{Play at headset?}
  B -->|No| C[OK — check periodically]
  B -->|Yes| D[Loosen locknut]
  D --> E[Turn adjusting cup to remove play]
  E --> F[Bars swing freely?]
  F -->|No — tight| G[Back off adjusting cup slightly]
  F -->|Yes| H[Hold cup — tighten locknut]
  G --> E
  H --> I[Re-test for play]
  I --> B




Figure 9.2: Threaded headset adjustment protocol.

title: 9  Steering and headset
text:
9.2 Integrated / threadless headsets
Most modern road bikes use a threadless system:

Loosen stem clamp bolts.
Turn the top cap bolt (usually 4 or 5 mm hex) to remove play — typically 0.2–0.5 Nm preload, just enough to seat the bearings.
Align the stem with the front wheel.
Torque stem clamp bolts evenly to manufacturer spec.







flowchart LR
  A[Loosen stem clamps] --> B[Tighten top cap to remove play]
  B --> C[Align stem]
  C --> D[Torque stem bolts to spec]
  D --> E[Check bearing feel]
